For it would be a very hard thing for us, to be subjected to the will of the ungodly, and not to have God caring for our wrongs. Peter, therefore, adorns God with this high attribute, that he judgeth righteously, as though he had said, “It behoves us calmly to bear evils; God in the meantime will not neglect what belongs to him, but will shew himself to be a righteous judge.” However wanton then the ungodly may be for a time, yet they shall not be unpunished for the wrongs done now to the children of God. Nor is there any cause for the godly to fear, as though they were without any protection; for since it belongs to God to defend them and to undertake their cause, they are to possess their souls in patience.
Moreover, as this doctrine brings no small consolation, so it avails to allay and subdue the inclinations of the flesh. For no one can recumb on the fidelity and protection of God, but he who in a meek spirit waits for his judgment; for he who leaps to take vengeance, intrudes into what belongs to God, and suffers not God to perform his own office. In reference to this Paul says, “Give place to wrath,” (Romans 12:19;) and thus he intimates that the way is closed up against God that he might not himself judge, when we anticipate him. He then confirms what he had said by the testimony of Moses, “Vengeance is mine.” (Deuteronomy 32:35.) Peter in short meant this, that we after the example of Christ shall be more prepared to endure injuries, if we give to God his own honor, that is, if we, believing him to be a righteous judge, refer our right and our cause to him.
It may however be asked, How did Christ commit his cause to the Father; for if he required vengeance from him, this he himself says is not lawful for us; for he bids us to do good to those who injure us, to pray for those who speak evil of us. (Matthew 5:44.) To this my reply is, that it appears evident from the gospel-history, that Christ did thus refer his judgment to God, and yet did not demand vengeance to be taken on his enemies, but that, on the contrary, he prayed for them, “Father,” he said, “forgive them.” (Luke 23:34.) And doubtless the feelings of our flesh are far from being in unison with the judgment of God. That any one then may commit his cause to him who judgeth righteously, it is necessary that he should first lay a check on himself, so that he may not ask anything inconsistent with the righteous judgment of God. For they who indulge themselves in looking for vengeance, concede not to God his office of a judge, but in a manner wish him to be an executioner. He then who is so calm in his spirit as to wish his adversaries to become his friends, and endeavors to bring them to the right way, rightly commits to God his own cause, and his prayer is, “Thou, O Lord, knowest my heart, how I wish them to be saved who seek to destroy me: were they converted, I should congratulate them; but if they continue obstinate in their wickedness, for I know that thou watchest over my safety, I commit my cause to thee.” This meekness was manifested by Christ; it is then the rule to be observed by us.
1 Peter 2:24-25
24. Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
24. Qui peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, ut peccatis mortui, justitiae vivamus: cujus livori sanati estis.
25. For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.
25. Eratis enim tanquam oves errantes; sed conversi estis nunc ad Pastorem et Episcopum animarum vestrarum.
entries.bbf9539a6d97877740c069e87f5dd0779c6f646d: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.2.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Pet.2.24" sID="gen135555" type="section"/> <div sID="gen135556" type="x-p"/>Had he commended nothing in Christ’s death except as an example, it would have been very frigid: he therefore refers to a fruit much more excellent. There are then three things to be noticed in this passage. The first is, that Christ by his death has given us an example of patience; the second, that by his death he restored us to life; it hence follows, that we are so bound to him, that we ought cheerfully to follow his example. In the third place, he refers to the general design of his death, that we, being dead to sins, ought to live to righteousness. And all these things confirm his previous exhortation.<div eID="gen135556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24</hi> <hi type="italic">Who his own self bare our sins</hi> This form of speaking is fitted to set forth the efficacy of Christ’s death. For as under the Law, the sinner, that he might be released from guilt, substituted a victim in his own place; so Christ took on himself the curse due to our sins, that he might atone for them before God. And he expressly adds, <hi type="italic">on the tree,</hi> because he could not offer such an expiation except on the cross. Peter, therefore, well expresses the truth, that Christ’s death was a sacrifice for the expiation of our sins; for being fixed to the cross and offering himself a victim for us, he took on himself our sin and our punishment. Isaiah, from whom Peter has taken the substance of his doctrine, employs various forms of expression, — that he was smitten by God’s hand for our sins, that he was wounded for our iniquities, that he was afflicted and broken for our sake, that the chastisement of our peace was laid on him. But Peter intended to set forth the same thing by the words of this verse, even that we are reconciled to God on this condition, because Christ made himself before his tribunal a surety and as one guilty for us, that he might suffer the punishment due to us.<div eID="gen135557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135558" type="x-p"/>This great benefit the Sophists in their schools obscure as much as they can; for they prattle that by the sacrifice of the death of Christ we are only freed after baptism from guilt, but that punishment is redeemed by satisfactions. But Peter, when he says that he bore our sins, means that not only guilt was imputed to him, but that he also suffered its punishment, that he might thus be an expiatory victim, according to that saying of the Prophet, “The chastisement of our peace was upon him.” If they object and say, that this only avails before baptism, the context here disproves them, for the words are addressed to the faithful.<div eID="gen135558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135559" type="x-p"/>But this clause and that which follows, <hi type="italic">by whose stripes ye were healed,</hi> may be also applied to the subject in hand, that is, that it behoves us to bear on our shoulders the sins of others, not indeed to expiate for them, but only to bear them as a burden laid on us.<div eID="gen135559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135560" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Being dead to sins</hi> <note n="34"> <div sID="gen135561" type="x-p"/> Or, “Being freed from sins:” <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀπογενόμενοι</foreign>, being away from, having departed from, or, being removed from. <hi type="italic">Beza</hi> renders it “being separated from.” Freedom from the power or dominion of sin seems more expressly to be intended, as the end of this freedom is, that we may live to righteousness; the end of forgiveness on the other hand is, that we may have peace with God. <hi type="italic">Beza, Estius, Grotis, </hi>and <hi type="italic">Scott, </hi>take this view of the sentence. The subject in hand is not the removal of guilt, but holiness of life, and Christ in his sufferings is set forth as the pattern to us. Then in what follows, our diseased state and our wandering from the right way, are the things referred to. Christ’s death was intended to answer two great ends, — to remove guilt and to remove or to destroy sin in us. The latter is the subject of this passage. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen135561" type="x-p"/> </note> He had before pointed out another end, even an example of patience; but here, as it has been stated, it is made more manifest, that we are to live a holy and righteous life. The Scripture sometimes mentions both, that is, that the Lord tries us with troubles and adversities, that we might be conformed to the death of Christ, and also that the old man has been crucified in the death of Christ, that we might walk in newness of life. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.10">Philippians 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.4">Romans 6:4</reference>.) At the same time, this end of which he speaks, differs from the former, not only as that which is general from what is particular; for in patience there is simply an example; but when he says that Christ suffered, that we being dead to sins should live to righteousness, he intimates that there is power in Christ’s death to mortify our flesh, as Paul explains more fully in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.6-Rom.6.14">the sixth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans</reference>. For he has not only brought this great benefit to us, that God justifies us freely, by not imputing to us our sins; but he also makes us to die to the world and to the flesh, that we may rise again to a new life: not that one day makes complete this death; but wherever it is, the death of Christ is efficacious for the expiation of sins, and also for the mortification of the flesh.<div eID="gen135560" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.2.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135555" osisID="1Pet.2.24" type="section"/>
entries.59b4d2029ed79d357cd4bb8841edcdc8ecf0e7ef:
25 For ye were as sheep This also has Peter borrowed from Isaiah, except that the Prophet makes it a universal statement,
“All we like sheep have gone astray.” (Isaiah 53:6.)
But on the word sheep there is no particular stress; he indeed compares us to sheep, but the emphasis is on what the Prophet adds, when he says that every one had turned to his own way. The meaning then is, that we are all going astray from the way of salvation, and proceeding in the way of ruin, until Christ brings us back from this wandering.
And this appears still more evident from the clause which follows, but are now returned to the Shepherd, etc.;
I would render the clause thus, “But you have been now restored,” that is, from your wandering, “to the shepherd and the bishop (or, overseer) of your souls.” Macknight thinks, that our Lord took the title of shepherd in order to shew that he is the person foretold in Ezekiel 34:23, and that Peter alludes, in calling him bishop or overseer, to the eleventh verse of that chapter, the latter clause of which, according to the Sept. is, “I will oversee them,” (ἐπισκέψομαι.) — Ed.
for all who are not ruled by Christ, are wandering like lost sheep in the ways of error. Thus, then, is condemned the whole wisdom of the world, which does not submit to the government of Christ. But the two titles given here to Christ are remarkable, that he is the Shepherd and Bishop of souls There is then no cause to fear, but that he will faithfully watch over the safety of those who are in his fold and under his care. And it is his office to keep us safe both in body and soul; yet Peter mentions only souls, because this celestial Shepherd keeps us under his own spiritual protection unto eternal life.
CHAPTER 3
1 Peter 3:1-4
1. Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives;
1. Similiter mulieres subjectae sint propriis maritis; ut etiam siqui sunt increduli sermoni, per uxorum conversationem absque sermone lucrifiant;
2. While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear.
2. Considerantes puram (vel, castam) vestram in timore conversationem;
3. Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
3. Quarum ornatus sit non externus, in plicatura capillorum et circumpositione auri, aut palliorum amictu;
4. But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
4. Sed interior cordis homo, qui in incorruptione situs est placidi et quieti spiritus, qui spiritus coram Deo pretiosus est (vel, quod est coram Deo pretiosum.)

entries.62e0e8851b9594abe21eded6c487a88c4ad62744:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="2" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. II.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 WHerefore <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Having in the former Chapter mentioned the new Birth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23. and exhorted to brotherly Love, as agreeable to it, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. he begins this Chapter with a Dehortation, wherein he disswades them from those Vices which are contrary to the state of regenerate Men in the general, and brotherly Love in particular.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 12.1.</ns0:note> laying aside <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>put off</ns0:hi>; a Metaphor from an old over-worn Garment, fit only to be thrown away; See <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.22. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.8, 9. <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 1.21.</ns0:note> all malice <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Malignity, when Men do evil to others voluntarily, and industriously, or delight in other Men's harms; See <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.29. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.31.</ns0:note>, and all guile <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">All Fraudulence and Impostures, and Circumventing of others in any kind.</ns0:note>, and hypocrisies <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">All flattering, and counterfeiting Friendship, and shewing love in words, and outward Carriage, when the Heart is otherwise affected. So <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 22. Christ calls them Hypocrites that flattered him, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16, 18.</ns0:note>, and envies <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Grieving at other Men's Welfare.</ns0:note>, and all evil speakings <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">All kind of Detraction.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 As new-born babes <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Pursuant to his Discourse, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.23. where he speaks of their new Birth, he here calls them <ns0:hi>new-born Babes</ns0:hi>; but that not in Opposition to those that are adult, or of full Age, as <ns0:hi>Hebr.</ns0:hi> 5.14. and 1 <ns0:hi>Corin.</ns0:hi> 3.1. but in Op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />opposition to their former corrupt and unregenerate state, in which they were destitute of all spiritual Life; and so this agrees, not only to young Converts, but generally to all regenerate Persons.</ns0:note> desire <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Being new-born Babes, act as such in earnestly desiring, and longing for that spiritual Nou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rishment, which is so needful for you, even as Children as soon as they come into the World, are lingring after the Breast.</ns0:note> the sincere milk of the word <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> may be rendred (and is by some) <ns0:hi>rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonable Milk,</ns0:hi> viz. such as is for the Soul, not for the Body; that whereby the Mind is nourished and strengthned; or <ns0:hi>wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy</ns0:hi> Milk, the Substantive from which it is derived properly, and first signifying <ns0:hi>Word,</ns0:hi> or Speech, and being used for the <ns0:hi>Word</ns0:hi> of God<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 4.12. But this not being proper <ns0:hi>English,</ns0:hi> our Translation renders it best, the <ns0:hi>Milk of the Word,</ns0:hi> i. e. the Word which is Milk: The Apostle useth an Adjective for a Substantive, but that Adjective doth not signifie the quality of the Subject <ns0:hi>(Milk)</ns0:hi> as the other <ns0:hi>(Sincere)</ns0:hi> doth, but the Subject of it self. The like Phrase we have, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 3.7. Gr. <ns0:hi>Female,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>wifish weaker Vessel,</ns0:hi> which we turn by the Substan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tive, <ns0:hi>Wise,</ns0:hi> who is said there to be the weaker Vessel. So that the Doctrine of the Gospel is here to be understood, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 55.1. and Believers are to be nourished by the same Word, as their Food, by which, as the seed, they are said to be begotten, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.23. This Milk of the Word is said to be <ns0:hi>sincere,</ns0:hi> i. e. pure, without mixture, or Adulteration, not blen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded, or diluted (as Vintners do by their Wine, to whose Practice <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> alludes, when he speaks of Men's corrupting the Word, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.17. and 4.2.) with human Fictions or Traditions. Infants love the Sweetness of their Mother's Milk, and desire it pure, as it is: Believers should desire the Word pure, as it is in it self, not mixed with any thing that may lessen its Sweetness, and hinder its Efficacy.</ns0:note>, that ye may grow thereby <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">That by the Word, as your spiritual Nourishment, ye may grow more in spiritual Life and Strength, till ye come to be perfect Men, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 If so be <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This doth not imply a doubting, but a supposition, as was before observed, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.17.</ns0:note> ye have tasted <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not lightly tasted by a bare ineffectual Knowledge, as <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.4. but experienced and perceived by the taste of your spiritual Palate; your spiritual Sense, and Ability to judge of spiritual things being restored to you, with your new Nature in your new Birth. He refers to <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 34.8. and possibly to <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 66.11.</ns0:note>, that the Lord <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Lord Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sus Christ, as appears by the next Verse.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> gracious <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Good, kind, or rather sweet: The same word is applied to Wine, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 5.39. The sense of the whole, is, If ye have by Faith received the Gospel as glad Tidings, and worthy of all Acceptation, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.15. and therein perceived, and experienced the sweetness of those Consolations which are in Christ Jesus, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.1. Or, (which is the same) how sweet he is, who, in the preaching of the Gospel, exhibits himself to your spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual Senses, to be fed upon, and tasted by you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 To whom <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To which Christ.</ns0:note> coming <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">By Faith, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> in whom believ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 6.35.44, 45. The word is in the Present Tense, the Apostle describing here not their first Conversion to Christ, but their present state, that they being in Christ, were daily coming to him in the continued Exercise of their Faith.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>as unto</ns0:hi> a living <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not only having Life in himself, but enlivening those that by Faith adhere to him.</ns0:note> stone <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> A Corner-Stone, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. Being about to set forth the Church, as a spiritual Building, he first mentions Christ as the Foundation, and Corner-Stone.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 118.22.</ns0:note> disallowed indeed of men <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Rejected, not only by the unbelieving <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and their Rulers formerly, but still by the unbelieving World.</ns0:note>, but cho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sen <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either chosen to be the Foundation of the Building, and then it is the same as fore-ordained, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.20. Or, chosen is the same as choice, excellent.</ns0:note> of God, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> precious <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">A different Expression of the same thing. Here seems to be an Allusion to those Stones which Men count precious, and have in great Esteem; and Christ's being precious in the sight of God, is set in Opposi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to his being disallowed of Men, to intimate, that their Unbelief, and rejecting Christ doth not make him less valuable in himself, when his Father so much honours him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Ye also as lively <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> as being enlivened by Christ. The word here trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lated, <ns0:hi>lively,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>living</ns0:hi> in the former Verse, is the same, but being there spoken of Christ, it is to be understood actively, and here being applied to Believers, who receive their spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual Life from Christ, it must be taken passively.</ns0:note> stones <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Each particular Believer is here called a Stone, as altogether an House or Temple, 2 <ns0:hi>Co.</ns0:hi> 6.16. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 2.21. and in respect of their Union among themselves, and with their Foundation; tho elsewhere in respect of God's Inhabitation, even parti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cular Believers are called his Temple, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.16, 17, and 6.19.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>be ye built.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> are built up <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> Upon Christ the principal Corner-Stone, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 2.20. This may be understood, either, 1. Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />paratively, <ns0:hi>q.d. be ye built up,</ns0:hi> and then it is an Exhorta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and relates not only to their continuing in Christ, but their being further built up on him by Faith, and is of the same Import as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>that ye may grow</ns0:hi>: Or rather, 2. Indica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tively; the Apostle as yet being engaged in shewing the Dig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nity and Priviledges of Believers, and not entring upon his Exhortation, till <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. The words being in the Present Tense, implies the Building to be still but going on, and not yet finished.</ns0:note> a spiritual <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 3.6.</ns0:note> house <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In distinction from the material one, relating to those Scriptures where the Tabernacle or Temple is cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led God's House, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 23.19. and 34.26. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23.18. The material House built of dead Stones, was but a Type of the spiritual House made up of lively Stones, and built upon Christ the living Stone; and this he brings (the Truth being always more excellent than the Type) to heigthen the Privi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledges of the Gospel-Church.</ns0:note>, an holy <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Isa. 61.6. and 66.21. v. 9.</ns0:note> priesthood <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either the Abstract is put for the Concrete, an holy Priesthood for holy Priests; or it may note the whole College or Society of Evangelical Priests, consisting of all particular Saints, to whom, in the New-Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stament, this Title is given, but never appropriated to Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel-Ministers: Christ being a Priest for ever after the Order of <ns0:hi>Melchisedec,</ns0:hi> had no Partner with him in his Priesthood, but was himself only to offer a Propitiatory Sacrifice to God for Sin. The immediate end of Gospel-Priests to offer, not bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dily, but spiritual Sacrifices in general themselves, whom they are to consecrate to God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.1. particularly Prayer, Thanksgivings, Alms, and other Duties of Religion, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.18. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.15, 16.</ns0:note>, to offer up <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Hos. 14.2. Mal. 1.11. Rom. 12.1.</ns0:note> spiritual sacrifices <ns0:hi>e</ns0:hi> acceptable unto God by Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">By, and through whom alone, as the Persons, so the Performances of Believers (tho in themselves imperfect) are pleasing to God, Christ presenting them to his Father by his Intercession, and covering their Defects by his own most perfect Righteousness. Some refer this clause, <ns0:hi>by Iesus Christ,</ns0:hi> to the fore-going Verb <ns0:hi>to offer up,</ns0:hi> and then the words run thus, <ns0:hi>to offer up spiritual Sacrifices by Iesus Christ, acceptable to God</ns0:hi>; but the former seems most proper, and includes this latter: we are therefore to offer up spiritual Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crifices to God by Christ, because they are acceptable only by him, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.21. compare with 15, 16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:582" />6 Wherefore also it is contained <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word being of an active form, makes great difference among Expositors about these words; not to trouble the Reader with variety, the plainest way of under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing them, seems to be, either, 1. That <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood here, and supplied out of the former Verse, <ns0:hi>Where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore God contains it in the Scripture:</ns0:hi> Or, 2ly. that the word, tho of an active Termination, be yet taken in a passive sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nification, <ns0:hi>contains,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>is contained,</ns0:hi> so our Translators do; and this way of speaking is not unusual with other Writers.</ns0:note> in the scripture, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 28.16. Rom. 9.32.</ns0:note> Behold <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">I the Lord, not Man, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 118.23.</ns0:note>, I lay <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> By the Preach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of the Gospel, wherein Christ was declared to be the only Foundation of the Church, and whereby Faith was wrought in the Hearts of Men, who were thereby actually built on Christ, as their Foundation, and so the spiritual House, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. erected.</ns0:note> in Sion <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either by Synechdoche, <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> (whereof <ns0:hi>Sion</ns0:hi> was a part) where by the preaching of Christ first, and the Apostles after his Ascension, and sending the Spirit, this Foundation-Stone was first laid, and God's Temple begun to be built, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 110.2. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 2.3. <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 4.2. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24.47. Or rather <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> here is to be understood of the Gospel-Church, whereof <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> was a Type.</ns0:note> a chief corner-stone <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Head of the Corner,</ns0:hi> Psalm 118.22. that which both supports the Building, and unites the Parts; Christ being the Foundation not of a part only, but of the whole Church; all the parts of which, Gentile, as well as <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> are jointly built on him, and upheld by him, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 2.20.</ns0:note>, elect, precious <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5.</ns0:note>: and he that believeth on him, shall not be confounded <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Shall not be disappointed of his expected Salvation, and so shall have no cause to be ashamed of his Hope. This is according to the LXX, the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> hath it, <ns0:hi>shall not make haste,</ns0:hi> i. e. he that believes in Christ shall not through haste, or Distrust, or Un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />willingness to wait God's time and way, seek after any other way of Salvation than by Christ; and so (as before) not being disappointed, shall have no cause to be ashamed; whereas they that do not believe, but make haste, coming short<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of their Expectation, are at last fill'd with Confusion. See the places in the Margin.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Unto you therefore which believe <ns0:hi>he is</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>an honour.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cious <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Margin reads it according to the <ns0:hi>Greek, an Honour,</ns0:hi> either the Abstract is put for the Concrete, <ns0:hi>an Honour,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>honourable,</ns0:hi> or precious (as the Text hath it) and then the sense is plain, that Christ, as he is precious in himself, and to his Father, so he is to them that believe: Or, <ns0:hi>Honour</ns0:hi> may be put for the cause of Honour, and then it is opposed to Shame and Confusion before-mentioned, and the sense is, Ye that believe, shall be so far from being ashamed, or having your Faith frustrated, that ye shall be honoured, and saved by Christ. And this agrees well with what follows in this and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8.</ns0:note>: but unto them which be disobedient <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Unbelievers, who were disobedient to the great Command of the Gospel concerning Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 118.22. Mat. 21.42. Acts 4.11.</ns0:note> the stone which the builders <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The High-Priests, Scribes, Pharisees, and Rulers of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> whose Duty it was to build up the Church, as having not only the Name, but the Power then residing in them.</ns0:note> disallowed <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Rejected him, and would not acknowledge him for the promised <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and the great Foundation upon which the Church of God was to be built.</ns0:note>, the same is made the head of the corner <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How is Christ said to be made the <ns0:hi>Head of the Corner</ns0:hi> to them that reject him? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Either, 1. something is here to be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood, <ns0:hi>viz. this is said,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>spoken,</ns0:hi> which follows, <ns0:hi>the Stone which the Builders,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>q.d.</ns0:hi> they despised him, but God hath honoured him; they would allow him no place in the Building, but God hath given him the best, made him the Head-stone of the Corner: Or, 2. Christ may be said to be made to the Disobedient in spite of their rejecting and opposing him, the Head of the Corner; <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> a King and a Judge to restrain, and curb them in, seeing they would not be ruled by him.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 8.14. Rom. 9.33.</ns0:note> And a stone of stumbling, and a <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">1 Cor. 1.23.</ns0:note> rock of offence <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">i. e. A Stone at which they stumble, a Rock at which they are offended; and so it implies Christ not to be the cause of their stumbling, but the Object of it; they of their own accord, and through the pravity of their Nature, without any just occasion given by him, being offended, either be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they find not that in him which they expected, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> outward Encouragements; or find that in him, which they do not like, the Holiness of his Law, and Purity of his Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine, contrary to their Corruptions and Lusts, and espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially his requiring of them Faith in him for the Justification of their Persons, which was so contrary to the Pride of their Hearts, and which was one great reason of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> stum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bling at him, as seeking to establish their own Righteousness, and therefore not submitting to the Righteousness of God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.32, 33. comp. with 10.3. This stumbling includes not only their falling into Sin, but into Destruction too, the Punishment of Sin, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 8.14, 15. whereof Christ can be no more than the inculpable occasion, but their own Unbelief the proper Cause.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even to them</ns0:hi> which stumble at the word, being disobedient <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">These words may have a double read<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, one according to our Translation, and then the sense is, that stumble at the Word of the Gospel, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> are disobedient to it, in rejecting Christ therein offered to them: Or, <ns0:hi>that stum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, being disobedient to the Word</ns0:hi>; i. e. stumble at Christ preached to them in the Word, and therefore will not obey it: they shew that they are offended at Christ, by their not receiving his Doctrine, nor accepting his offers.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Exod. 9.16. Rom. 9.22. Jude 4.</ns0:note> whereunto <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either this may refer, 1. to <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. where Christ is said to be <ns0:hi>laid</ns0:hi> (the same word in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> with that which is here trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lated, by <ns0:hi>appointed) in Zion,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>a chief Corner-stone, elect and precious,</ns0:hi> on whom whosoever <ns0:hi>blieveth, shall not be confounded:</ns0:hi> The Apostle then adds, that even these Unbelievers were <ns0:hi>appointed (viz.</ns0:hi> in their external Vocation, as being taken in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to Covenant with God) to be built on Christ by Faith, but they stumbled, by their Unbelief, at the Word of the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel, and consequently at this stumbling-Stone. And then it is an high aggravating the Unbelief of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> that they be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing God's peculiar People, should reject that Salvation which was sent to them, and to the first offer of which they were designed, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 13.26, 46, 47. Or, 2ly. to the words im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mediately going before, <ns0:hi>that stumble at the Word, being diso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedient,</ns0:hi> and then the sense is (speaking concerning the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />probate <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi>) that God appointed them to this stumbling, in his decreeing not to give them Faith in Christ, but to leave them to their Unbelief, and to punish them justly for it: See <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.17. and 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.9. <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 4. The Scope of the Apostle in this whole Verse seems to be, to keep weak Christians from being offended at the multitude of Unbelie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers, and especially at their seeing Christ rejected by the Jewish Rulers and Doctors; and this he doth by pointing them to the Scripture, where all this was long since fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />told, and therefore not to be wondred at now, nor be any occasion of offence to them. See the like, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 16.1, 4.</ns0:note> also they were appointed.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 But ye <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Ye Believers, in opposition to those Reprobates that are disobedient to the Word. He shews that those Dignities and Priviledges, which were mentioned by <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> as belonging to their Fore-fathers, did much more belong to them; and that they had the real Exhibition in Christ, of those good Things whereof their Fathers had but a taste, and which the rest of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had lost by their Unbelief.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> a chosen generation <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">A People chosen of God, not only out of the World, but from among the rest of your own Nation, and not only to an external Adop<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and outward Priviledges, (as the whole Body of the Nation was) but to eternal Salvation.</ns0:note>, a <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rev. 1.6. and 5.10.</ns0:note> roy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al priesthood <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Kingdom of Priests.</ns0:hi> He called them an holy Priesthood, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. now he calls them a Royal Priesthood, to shew that they were made not only spiritual Priests, but spiritual Kings; which Priviledge they had not as <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> but as Believers, who are all of them as Priests in respect of God to whom they are consecrated, and to whom they offer up spiritual Sacrifices; so Kings in respect both of their Enemies over whom they are victori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous, and of the Kingdom they are hereafter to inherit.</ns0:note>, an holy nation <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> calls your Fathers an holy Nation, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 7.6. in re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect of their Separation from the Impurities of the Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles, their Dedication to God, and the many Laws. God gave them, obliging them to external and ceremonial Purity, whereby they were admonished of internal and real Holiness; but ye are an holy Nation in respect of that true and inward Holiness it self, whereof that ceremonial Holiness was but a Signification. He seems particularly to allude to <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 62.12.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>a purchased people.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> a peculiar people <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 19.5. it is a <ns0:hi>peculiar Treasure</ns0:hi>; and so the same word is rendred, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.5. and a <ns0:hi>special People,</ns0:hi> Deut. 7.6. <ns0:hi>a pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culiar People,</ns0:hi> and 14.2. The word used by the LXX implying as much, but <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 3.17. where we render it, <ns0:hi>Iewels</ns0:hi>; the LXX use the same word which <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> doth here, which is as much as <ns0:hi>a People of Acquisition,</ns0:hi> or which God hath acquired to himself for his peculiar Possession or Treasure. God had rescued the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> from their <ns0:hi>Egyptian</ns0:hi> Bondage, and taken them to be his peculiar People above all others, and claimed a Right to them, and counted them precious, as having redeemed them with a strong Hand, and got Posses<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of them at the expence of so much Power, and so many Miracles. This Deliverance of theirs, was the Type of Christ's delivering the Church from the Tyranny of Satan, the spiritual <ns0:hi>Pharaoh,</ns0:hi> and the World, the spiritual <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> and a state of Sin, the worst Bondage; upon the account whereof, God's People are called <ns0:hi>a Peculiar People,</ns0:hi> or a People thus ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 2.14. and <ns0:hi>a purchased Possession,</ns0:hi> Ephes. 1.14. where the same word is likewise used.</ns0:note>; that <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This notes the end of all these Priviledges vouchsafed them, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That they should glorifie God in the Enjoyment of them. He seems to refer to <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 43.7, 21. <ns0:hi>This People have I formed for my self,</ns0:hi> (or acquired, as the LXX hath it) <ns0:hi>they shall shew forth my Praise.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> ye should shew forth <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Publish, and declare both in Words and Deeds, that others may be excited to glorifie God in the like man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner.</ns0:note> the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>virtues.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> praises <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Virtues,</ns0:hi> that Wisdom, Power, Goodness, Righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness, Truth, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which God haht manifested in his Vouchsafements to you, and in the Acknowledgment of which he may be glorified.</ns0:note> of him, who hath called <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">By an effectual Calling, according to his purpose, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.28.</ns0:note> you <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 5.8. Col. 1.13.</ns0:note> out of darkness <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Darkness of Ignorance, Unbelief, Sin, and Misery. The time before the Publication of the Gospel, was a time of Darkness, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 4.16. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 1.79.</ns0:note> into his marvellous light <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Light of Knowledge, Faith, Holi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, Comfort. See <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 5.8. It is called <ns0:hi>marvellous,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause Men see what they never saw before; <ns0:hi>wonderful Things out of God</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> Psalm 119.18. and because it is a marvel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lous thing that they who sate in so gross Darkness, should be translated into so glorious a Light.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:582" />10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hos. 1.9, 10. and 2.23. Rom. 9.25.</ns0:note> Which in time past <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> not a people <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either were not a People, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> a formed State, or Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monwealth, being dispersed in several Countries among o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther People, and not worth the Name of a People: Or, were not the People of God (supplying <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> out of the op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posite clause) since he had given them a Bill of Divorce, and said, <ns0:hi>lo Ammi,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>lo Ruhamah</ns0:hi> to them, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 2. These were the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> of the Dispersion, and such as had not returned out of the <ns0:hi>Babylonish</ns0:hi> Captivity, together with many of other Tribes mixed with them, who, before their Conversion to Christ, seemed cut off from the Body of that People, had no solemn Worship of God among them, and were tainted with the Corruptions of the Heathen, with whom they conversed.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> now the people of God <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Really God's People restored to their old Covenant-state, and Church-Priviledges, by their believing in Christ.</ns0:note>, which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The Mercy of being God's People, and enjoying their Priviledges, being justified, at peace with God, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Lest they might any way abuse what he had said in the former Verse concerning their great Dignity and Priviledges, so as to ascribe any thing to themselves, the Apostle intimates here, that all they enjoyed, was meerly out of God's Mercy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Dearly beloved, I beseech <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi> as stran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers and pilgrims <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not only Strangers in the several Countries where ye in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />habit, (being out of your own Land) but Strangers in the World, as all Believers are, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 39.12. and 119.19. and 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 29.15. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.13, 14.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 13.14. Gal. 5.16.</ns0:note> abstain from fleshly lusts <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Not only sensual De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sires, but all the Works of the Flesh, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.19, 20, 21. the carnal Mind it self being <ns0:hi>Enmity</ns0:hi> against God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.7.</ns0:note>, which war <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As Enemies, oppose, and fight against, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.23. <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 4.1.</ns0:note> against the soul <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The inner Man, or regenerate part, or Spirit, which is op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed to fleshly Lusts. See <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.17.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 8.21. Chap. 3.16.</ns0:note> Having your conversation honest <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Irreprehensible, fruitful, such as may gain Men's Love, and commend the Religion you profess.</ns0:note> among the Gentiles <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Who, by reason of their differing from your Religion, are the more like to observe you. This proves this Epistle to be written to the <ns0:hi>Iews.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: that <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>wherein.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> whereas they speak against you as evil doers, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 5.16.</ns0:note> they may by <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> good works which they shall behold, glorifie God <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Not only think more favourably of you, but of your Religion; acknowledge the Grace of God in you, and more readily subject themselves to him, (the best way of glorifying him) it being usual with God to make way for the Conversion of Sinners by the holy Conversation of Saints.</ns0:note> in the day of visitation <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> a gracious Visitation, when God calls them by the Gospel to the Knowledge of Christ, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 1.68, 78. and 7.16. and 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.44.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 13.1.</ns0:note> Submit your selves to every <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Of all kinds, whether Supreme, or subordinate.</ns0:note> ordinance of man <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>Human Creatures</ns0:hi> which may be understood, either as <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 16.15. every Human Creature for every Man only restrain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing it to the present Subject whereof he treats, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gistrates, and the sense is, to every Magistrate: Or rather, (though to the same effect) <ns0:hi>to every Human Ordinance</ns0:hi>; or, as we translate it, <ns0:hi>Ordinance of Man</ns0:hi>; the word, <ns0:hi>Creature,</ns0:hi> being taken for an Ordinance, or Constitution, and creating for <ns0:hi>ordaining,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>appointing</ns0:hi>; so <ns0:hi>Oecumenius</ns0:hi> will have the word to signifie, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 2.15. to <ns0:hi>make</ns0:hi> of twain, one new Man. But this Creature, or Ordinance here is to be understood of the Magistrate (as appears by the following words) which is called <ns0:hi>Human,</ns0:hi> not as if Magistracy were not an Ordinance of God, (for <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.1. the Powers that are, are said to be <ns0:hi>ordained of God</ns0:hi>) but, either because it is only among Men, and proper to them; or because it is of Man secondarily, and instrumentally, tho of God primarily, and originally; God making use of the Ministry of Men in bringing them into the Magistracy; as tho Church-Officers are God's Ordinance, yet he makes use of Men to put them into Office.</ns0:note> for the Lord's sake <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For God's sake, who commands this Obedience, and gave them their Authority, and is represented by them, and honoured by that Obedience which is yielded to them in all things a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />greeable to his Will. The Phrase seems to be of the same import with that of being obedient in the Lord, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 6.1.</ns0:note>: whether it be to the king <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To <ns0:hi>Cesar</ns0:hi> the then Supreme Magistrate, under whose Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risdiction the Jewish Christians were; and this being a gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral Command extending to all Christians, it follows, that O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedience is due from them to those Chief Magistrates, whose Subjects respectively they are.</ns0:note> as supreme <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not only above the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, but above other Magistrates.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Or unto governours <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He seems immediately to intend the Governours of Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vinces under the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Emperors, such as <ns0:hi>Pilate, Felix, Fe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slus,</ns0:hi> were in <ns0:hi>Iudea; Sergius Paulus</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Cyprus,</ns0:hi> Acts 13.7. and other Places: See <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 3.1. but so as to imply, under the Name of Governours, all inferior Magistrates, as under the Name of King, he doth all Supreme.</ns0:note>, as unto them that are sent by him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either, 1. by the King, or Supreme Magistrate, and then the next words shew what should be his end in sending, or appointing Of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ficers, or subordinate Rulers under him: Or, 2. rather sent by God, from whom all Rulers subordinate, as well as Su<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />preme, have their Authority, and which is the great Motive on which they are to be obeyed; and then the following words shew what is God's end in appointing them, and ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther reason for yielding Obedience to them, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> their being set up for the common Good of the Societies which they rule.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 13.4.</ns0:note> for the punishment of evil-doers, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 13.3.</ns0:note> for the praise <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Praise is a kind of Reward, and is here to be taken by a Synechdoche for all sorts of Rewards given to those that do well, and are obedient to the Laws. See <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.3, 4.</ns0:note> of them that do well.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 For so is the will of God <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">His Command.</ns0:note>, that with <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Tit. 2.8.</ns0:note> well-doing <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">All manner of Offices of Humanity, whereof Obedience to Magistrates is a principle one.</ns0:note> ye may put to silence <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>muzzle,</ns0:hi> stop the mouths, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.11. <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> by taking away all oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of evil-speaking.</ns0:note> the ig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />norance <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either their Ignorance of the State, and Conversation of Believers, which may be the occasion of their speaking evil of them; or their Ignorance of God and his ways, to which Christ imputes the Fury of Perfecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tors, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 16.3. They that know not God themselves, are most ready to reproach and slander those that do.</ns0:note> of foolish men <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">True Wisdom consisting in the Knowledge of God; they that are destitute of that Knowledge, as Unbelievers are, are called foolish.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 5.1, 13.</ns0:note> As free <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">He prevents an Objection; they might pretend they were a free People, as <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and therefore were not to obey Strangers, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 17.15. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.33. and made free by Christ. He answers, That they were free indeed, but it was from Sin, and not from Righteousness, not from Obedience to God's Law, which requires Subjection to Magistrates, for they were still the Servants of God.</ns0:note>, and not <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Gr. or <ns0:hi>having.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> using <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> liberty for a cloke of maliciousness <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not using your Liberty to cover, or palliate your VVickedness, excusing your selves from Obedience to your Superiours by a pretence of Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian Liberty, when, tho ye be free from Sin, yet ye are not from Duty.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">1 Cor. 7.22.</ns0:note> but as the ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants of God <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And so still bound to obey him, and your Ru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lers in him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>esteem.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Honour all men <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> according a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Honour is due to them, according to their Dignity, Powe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Gifts, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.10. and 13.7. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.3.</ns0:note>: Love the brother<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hood <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Tho all may challenge sutable<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Respects, yet there is a more special affection owing to Believers, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.22. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.10.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 22.21.</ns0:note> Fear God <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">With a filial fear or reverence. This command is interposed, either to shew what is the true Spring and Fountain, from which all the Duties we per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />form to Men, are to proceed, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Fear of God, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause where that doth not prevail, no Duty to Men can be rightly performed, (they love the Brotherhood best, and honour the Kings most, that truly Fear God) or to shew the due bounds of all the Offices we perform to Men, that nothing is to be done for them which is inconsistent with the Fear of God.</ns0:note>: Honour the King <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">With that honour which is peculiarly due to him above all others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:583" />18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 3.22. Tit. 2.9.</ns0:note> Servants be subject to <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> masters with all fear <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Not only reverence of Masters, and fear of offending them is to be understood, but Fear of God, as appears by the parallel place, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.22. see <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.5, 6, 7.</ns0:note>, not only to the good <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Good</ns0:hi> he means not gracious or holy, but, as the next word explains it, Gentle, Just, Equal.</ns0:note> and gentle, but also to the froward <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rose, Crabbed, Unjust, Unmerciful.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The word is not the same which <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> useth, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.22. but may well comprehend the Servants he speaks of, as implying not only Slaves, but those that were made free, yet continued still in the Family; and so signifies Servants of whatsoever condition.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 For this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>thank.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 5.10.</ns0:note> thank-worthy <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">In the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> (as in the Margin) the Substantive is put for the Adjective; the sence is either, this is acceptable to God, and will be graciously rewarded by him; or, this is praise-worthy, and will be your Glory, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20.</ns0:note>, if a man for conscience toward God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Out of respect to God, and a desire of pleasing him.</ns0:note> endure grief, suffer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing wrongfully.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 3.14. and 4.14, 15.</ns0:note> what glory <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">What praise or glory do ye get by it? Or, what great matter do you do? this Interrogation hath the force of a negation, but is to be understood comparatively; it is worthy of praise to suffer patiently, even when Men suffer justly, but worthy of little, in comparison of suffering pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiently when unjustly.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>is it</ns0:hi> if when ye be buf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if when ye do well and suffer <ns0:hi>for it,</ns0:hi> ye take it patiently, this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>thank.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> acceptable with God <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This shews what is meant by thank-worthy, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19. and the Apostle adds what kind of thanks or praise he intends, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> not that which is of Man (which many times may fail, even when Men patiently suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fer injuries) but that which is of God, to which Believers should especially have respect.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 16.24. 1 Thess. 3.3.</ns0:note> even hereunto <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> To patient bearing of Sufferings, even for well-do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing.</ns0:note> were ye called <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> to Christ and the fellowship of his Kingdom; <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> your very Calling and Profession, as Christians, requires this of you.</ns0:note> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Chap. 3.18.</ns0:note> Christ also <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">There is an Emphasis in this particle, it is as much as if he had said, even Christ our Lord and Head hath suffered for us, and therefore we that are but his Servants and Members must not think to escape Sufferings.</ns0:note> suffered for <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Some read <ns0:hi>for you.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> us <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, as in the Margin, <ns0:hi>for you,</ns0:hi> which agrees with the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning and end of the Verse, where the second Person is used; but most read it as we do in the First Person, and the sence is still the same; only the Apostle from a ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral Proposition draws a particular Exhortation; Christ suffered for us (therein he comprehends the Saints to whom he writes) and left an Example for us all; do ye there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore to whom, as well as to others, he left this Example, follow his Steps, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 13.15. and 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.6.</ns0:note> leaving us an example <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">As of other graces, so especially of Patience.</ns0:note> that ye should follow his steps.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 53.9. 2 Cor. 5.21.</ns0:note> Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This signifies Christ's absolute Perfection, in that he did not of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fend so much as with his mouth, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 3.2. The sense is, Christ was free from all manner of Sin, and yet he suffer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed patiently; and therefore well may ye be content to suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fer too, though wrongfully; seeing though ye may be in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nocent in your sufferings, yet you come so far short of Christ's perfection.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> There was no guile in his mouth, it is an Hebraism, to <ns0:hi>be found</ns0:hi> is the same as <ns0:hi>to be,</ns0:hi> and not <ns0:hi>to be found,</ns0:hi> the same as <ns0:hi>not to be, Gen.</ns0:hi> 2.20. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 39.2. see <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.10.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 27.39. Joh. 8.48, 49.</ns0:note> Who when he was reviled <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">By Christ's being reviled, we are to understand all those injurious Words, Reproaches, Slanders, Blasphemies, which his Persecutors cast out against him.</ns0:note> reviled net again <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Therefore when he told the Jews they were of their Father the De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vil, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.44. that was not a reviling them, but a just accusation of them, or reproof of their Devilish behaviour.</ns0:note>, when he suffered <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">When he was affected not only with verbal but real in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />juries, buffeted, spit upon, crowned with Thorns, crucifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:note> he threatned not <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He was so far from avenging himself, or recompen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cing Evil for Evil; that he did not so much as threaten what he would afterward do to them.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>committed his cause.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> committed <ns0:hi>himself</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>his cause,</ns0:hi> as in the Margin; neither is in the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> but either may be well supplied, and to the same purpose the sence is, Christ did not retaliate, nor act any thing out of private Revenge, but so referr'd himself, and the judgment of his Cause to his Father's good Pleasure, as rather to desire Pardon for his Persecutors, than Vengeance on them, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 23.34. The Apostle adds this of God's judging righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ously, for the comfort of Servants to whom he speaks, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.8, 9. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.24. and 4.1. and for the terror of Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters, that the former might learn patience, and the latter moderation.</ns0:note> to him that judgeth righteously.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 8.17.</ns0:note> Who his own self <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not by offering any other Sacrifice (as the Levitical Priests did) but by that of himself.</ns0:note> bare our sins <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>took up,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>lifted up,</ns0:hi> in allusion to the Sacrifices of the Old Testament, the same word being used of them, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 7.27. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 2.21. As the Sins of the Offerer were typically laid upon the Sacri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fice, which, being substituted in his place, was likewise slain in his stead; so Christ standing in our room, took up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on him the guilt of our Sins, and bare their Punishment, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53.4. &c. The Lord laid on him our iniquities, and he willingly took them up; and by bearing their Curse, took away our guilt. Or, it may have respect to the Cross, on which Christ being lifted up (<ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 3.14, 15. & 12.32.) took up our Sins with him, and expiated their guilt by un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dergoing that Death which was due to us for them.</ns0:note> in his own body <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This doth not exclude his Soul, but is rather to be understood, by a Synecdoche, of his whole human Nature, and we have the Sufferings of his Soul mentioned, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53.10, 12. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 12.27.) but mention is made of his Body, because the Sufferings of that were most visible.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="Verbar" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>to.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> on the tree <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">On the Cross.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 6.2, 11. and 7.6.</ns0:note> that we being dead unto sin should live <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther end of Christ's Death, the mortification of Sin, and our being freed from the Dominion of it, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.2, 6. and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing reformed to a Life of Holiness.</ns0:note> unto righteousness, by whose stripes ye were healed <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> of the Wound made in your Souls by Sin; this seems to relate to the Blows that Servants might receive of Cruel Masters, against which the Apostle comforts them, and to the patient bear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of which he exhorts them, because Christ by bearing Stripes (a servile punishment) under which may be com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prehended all the Sufferings of his Death, had healed them of much worse Wounds, and Spiritual Diseases, the guilt of their Consciences, and the defilement of their Souls.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 For ye were <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">While ye continued in your Judaism, and had not yet received the Gospel.</ns0:note> as sheep going astray <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">From Christ the great Shepherd, and the Church of Believers his Flock, and the way of righteousness in which he leads them. Ye were alienated from the Life of God, bewildred and lost in the way of Sin, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53.6.</ns0:note>, but are now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 37.24. Heb. 13.20.</ns0:note> returned to the Shepherd <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In your Conversion to the Faith.</ns0:note>, and Bi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shop <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Christ the good Shepherd, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 10. that takes care of Souls, as a Shepherd doth of his Sheep.</ns0:note> of your Souls.<ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Superintendent, Inspector, or, as the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> phrase it, Visitor, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He that with Care looks to, inspects, and visits the Flock. This he adds for the Comfort (as of all Believers, so) particularly of Servants, that even they, as mean as they were, and as much expo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed to injuries, yet were under the care and tuition of Christ.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
